Goldeye rockfish (Sebastes thompsoni) attain a maximum recorded total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that places them among the medium-bodied members of the genus Sebastes in the North Pacific. Field surveys along the Japanese coast have consistently documented this ultimate length in older individuals, providing a reliable benchmark for asymptotic size in demographic models. The species exhibits a relatively slow growth trajectory typical of many rockfishes, with individuals adding somatic tissue incrementally over many years. This protracted growth pattern is reflected in the relationship between length and mass; for instance, the estimated wet weight of an individual at the ultimate length is approximately 503 grams [Wwi = approximately 503 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions calibrated for the genus. Such data are critical for understanding the energetic demands placed upon adults in the cold, productive waters they inhabit.

Reproductive maturation in Goldeye rockfish occurs at a notably smaller body size relative to the species' maximum. Puberty is initiated when individuals reach a total length of 16 centimeters [Lp = 16 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 66.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 66.9 grams] based on established morphometric relationships for the species. This size at first maturation suggests that females begin investing in reproductive tissues well before they approach their asymptotic dimensions, a strategy common among iteroparous marine teleosts. The relatively modest body mass at puberty implies that early reproductive events may be energetically constrained, yet the species persists through a strategy of repeated, low-volume spawning events over a lengthy adult lifespan.

The viviparous reproductive mode of Sebastes thompsoni presents unique challenges for quantifying early life stages. At the moment of parturition, newly released larvae have an extremely small body mass, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams]. This minuscule size, equivalent to a fraction of a milligram, is consistent with the small egg diameter observed in the genus and reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo during gestation. The larvae emerge in a relatively undeveloped state and must immediately begin exogenous feeding in the plankton. This early life history strategy contrasts sharply with that of demersal-spawning teleosts that produce larger, more energy-rich eggs.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized under controlled thermal conditions, providing insight into its maximum fecundity. At a stable water temperature of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C], females produce approximately 49,000 offspring per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 49,000 offspring per spawning event] and complete one spawning cycle per year [F_R_i = one spawning cycle per year]. This estimate, derived from comparative studies with the congener Sebastes inermis, accounts for both batch size and spawning frequency over the reproductive season. The temperature dependence of this process is critical, as deviations from this optimal thermal regime can significantly alter the timing and magnitude of larval production. Such data are essential for parameterizing population dynamics models under varying climatic scenarios.

Longevity data for Goldeye rockfish indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] when maintained at 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C], a duration that translates to roughly 10,950 days under these stable thermal conditions. This exceptional longevity is characteristic of many rockfishes and is linked to their slow somatic growth, late maturity, and low natural mortality rates in the adult stage. Comparative analyses with other Sebastes species suggest that this lifespan is at the upper end of the range observed for medium-sized members of the genus. The extended reproductive window afforded by such a long life allows females to compensate for the relatively low fecundity per spawning event by accumulating many reproductive bouts over decades, a life-history strategy that buffers the population against recruitment variability.
